## Paper

## Abstract

High entropy spinel oxides provide a versatile platform for electrocatalysis because multiple metal cations can be incorporated into a single crystalline lattice, enabling tunable electronic structures. However, controlling how these cations distribute between tetrahedral and octahedral coordination sites remains a major challenge, limiting rational catalyst design. Here, we modulate cation coordination site occupancy between tetrahedral and octahedral sites in a Co–Fe–Cr–Mn–Ni framework by introducing a sixth cation (Zn, Ga, Mg, or Al) with distinct site preference energies. Using density functional theory, synchrotron X-ray absorption spectroscopy, and magnetic circular dichroism, we demonstrate that Zn preferentially occupies tetrahedral sites, driving increased octahedral occupancy of cobalt. This redistribution increases the population of octahedrally coordinated cobalt in mixed oxidation states, enhances electrical conductivity, and improves oxygen evolution reaction activity. Our findings establish coordination site occupancy as a critical design parameter, providing a strategic pathway for tailoring multicomponent spinel electrocatalysts with optimized performance.

---

## Introduction

High-entropy materials (HEMs), distinguished by entropy-driven phase stabilization and compositional complexity, have rapidly emerged as versatile functional materials across applications in energy storage and conversion.1–5 A common assumption is that equimolar mixing of metal precursors yields a single-phase solid solution with uniformly distributed cations. This assumption is often supported by bulk-level characterizations such as X-ray diffraction (XRD) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mapping in transmission electron microscopy (TEM).6 However, recent studies employing advanced techniques have challenged this view. For example, high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have been shown to exhibit nanoscale chemical heterogeneity and element al clustering, indicating that equimolar input does not guarantee atomic-scale homogeneity.7,8 In parallel, site engineering and vacancy control have been actively explored in various HEMs to tailor functionalities including mechanical strength, electrical properties, and catalytic activity.9–14 Notable efforts include short-range ordering in HEAs,15,16 oxygen vacancy tuning in rock salt-type high-entropy oxides (HEOs),10,17,18 and B-site modulation in perovskite-type HEOs.19,20 These studies have expanded our understanding of how compositional complexity can be harnessed to control materials’ behavior. However, much less is understood about site-specific occupation in more complex structures, where the interplay between multiple crystallographic sites adds further degrees of freedom, and complexity.

Spinel-type HEOs are a particularly intriguing structure, featuring two distinct cation sites—tetrahedral (T ) and octahedral (O ) in a 1:2 ratio—whose occupancy is governed by oxidation states, ionic radii, and electronic configurations.21–23 This dual-site nature enables additional avenues for property tuning, but also complicates the control of cation distribution.24 Most conventional techniques lack the resolution to distinguish between T and O site occupancies at the bulk level, and few studies have demonstrated the importance of site-specific cation engineering in high-entropy spinel oxides (HESOs).25,26 Adjusting the occupancy of Co between O and T sites was shown to tune Co-O bond polarity and hence enhance redox kinetics in lithium-sulfur batteries.27,28 Separately, compositional tuning in HESOs with selective redistribution of transition metals across crystallographic sites has enabled control over ferrimagnetic ordering.29 Despite growing interest in HESOs for different applications,21,22,24,26–39 there remains a lack of direct correlation between synthetic composition, cation site distribution, and catalytic properties. Establishing such correlations would provide substantial strategies for catalyst design through targeted site engineering.

In this study, we address the gap in understanding and controlling coordination site distribution in HESOs, arising from the structural complexity of dual T and O sites, limited site-specific characterization techniques, and the lack of established correlations between composition, site occupancy, and catalytic performance. We introduce a strategy based on a targeted addition of site-selective cations (Zn, Ga, Al, or Mg) into a Co–Fe–Cr–Mn–Ni HESO framework to modulate the occupancy of key active elements (e.g., Co and Fe) between T and O sites. The high configuration entropy stabilized HESO lattice allows dopant introduction to drive significant Co migration without compromising structural stability due to multiple redox-active and redox-stable transition metals that collectively buffer the charge redistribution. We use synchrotron-based spectroscopy and density functional theory (DFT), showing that compositional design governs site-specific cation occupancy that influences electronic structure and electrocatalytic properties. Particularly, Zn addition promotes the redistribution of active cations into octahedral sites with more favorable adsorption energetics and higher electrical conductivity, which correlates with the improved oxygen evolution reaction (OER) activity. This establishes coordination site occupancy as a key design parameter and offers a broadly applicable strategy for tuning functionality in multicomponent electrocatalysts.

---

## Results

Design and Structural Characterization of High-Entropy Spinel Oxides
Fig. 1 illustrates cation engineering in HESOs with detailed structural characterization. All HESOs were synthesized using the previously reported solution-flame synthesis method with fast heating/cooling rates and high temperature, facilitating rapid single-phase formation.40 Our reference HESO comprises equimolar Co–Fe–Cr–Mn–Ni. Typically, these metal cations are assumed to be evenly distributed in both O and T sites (Fig. 1a),29,40 but detailed material characterizations, discussed later, reveal that the total cations are equimolar but they have uneven distributions in O and T sites.29,41 This uneven distribution is caused by site preference energies for various cations in spinel structures calculated from the crystal field theory.42 Cations with more positive energy (e.g., Zn2+) prefer the T site, and cations with more negative energy (e.g., Cr3+) prefer the O site (Fig. 1b).41 Thus, HESO does not have equimolar cations on O and T sites, presenting an opportunity to control configurational entropy by achieving a more uniform cation distribution on both T and O sites, leading to more stable structure. Our strategy is to intentionally introduce additional cations with distinct site preference energies to force the original cations into other sites. In our Co–Fe–Cr–Mn–Ni HESO, Ni and Cr exhibit strong O site preference, while Co, Fe, and Mn have more flexible coordination. As we incorporate a sixth element into the HESO: Zn (favoring T ), Al (favoring O ), and Ga/Mg (flexible occupancy),41 the distribution of Co–Fe–Cr–Mn–Ni in O and T sites is finely tuned.

For Zn-HESO, we expect that Zn prefers T sites, and more Co will be distributed to O sites (Fig. 1c). The as-synthesized Zn-HESO maintains a spinel structure with clear identification of O and T sites, as shown by high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) imaging along [110] zone axis (Fig. 1d, Supplementary Fig. 1). The cations in Zn-HESO exhibit uniform distribution as shown by HAADF-STEM-EDS (energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy) mapping (Fig. 1e, Supplementary Fig. 2).

Zn-HESO in high-resolution TEM images in Fig. 1f shows d-spacings of 0.246 nm for the (311) and 0.292 nm for the (220) planes, compared with those of reference spinel NiFe O (0.251 nm for (311) and 0.295 nm for (220)) and pristine HESO (0.250 nm for (311) and 0.294 nm for (220)). This corresponds to an overall lattice contraction of approximately 1–2%. Such contraction is consistent with the incorporation of Zn ions, which preferentially occupy T sites in spinel lattices, replacing or redistributing larger divalent cations (e.g., Mn2+) within the T sublattice, thereby reducing the average metal–oxygen bond length. Similar variations in d-spacing are observed locally, as highlighted in the inset of Fig. 1f, where the measured d-spacings span 0.23–0.27 nm for the (311) and 0.27–0.32 nm for the (220) planes, reflecting compositional and local structural heterogeneity intrinsic to high-entropy spinels. In contrast, Ga-, Mg-, and Al-substituted HESOs exhibit slightly different average d-spacings, with values of 0.254–0.263 nm for the (311) and 0.291–0.297 nm for the (220) planes (Supplementary Figs. 3–5). These differences reflect variations in the average cation distribution and site-specific ionic radii within the spinel lattice. For Ga3+ and Mg2+, which possess relatively larger ionic radii compared to some of the host cations in O or T coordination, subtle lattice expansion or reduced contraction may occur depending on their preferred coordination environment. Notably, Al-HESO shows a distinct behavior compared to Ga- and Mg-containing samples. Al3+ ions have a relatively small ionic radius in O coordination (~0.535 Å) and form strong Al–O bonds, which can locally stabilize the spinel framework without necessarily inducing uniform lattice contraction. As a result, the observed d-spacing in Al-HESO likely reflects a balance between local lattice distortion, cation redistribution, and strong metal–oxygen bonding, rather than a simple ionic-size-driven expansion or contraction.

X-ray diffraction (XRD) (Fig. 1g, Supplementary Fig. 6) also shows that both pristine and Zn-HESO maintain pure spinel structures. Zn-HESO shows a slight shift in (311) due to the lattice contraction from a smaller ionic radius of Zn. The fast Fourier transform (FFT) in Fig. 1f confirms that the diffraction pattern matches the expected spinel structure and is consistent with XRD results, and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) (Supplementary Figs. 7–9) shows near-equimolar ratios of Co–Fe–Cr–Mn–Ni with additional substituent (Zn, Ga, Mg, or Al), similar to the precursor ratios, at the surface.

Characterization of Electronic Structures for M-HESOs
To assess oxidation states and local coordination of M-HESOs, X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) K-edge measurements, including X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) and extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS), were performed at 3d transition metals K-edges (Supplementary Figs. 10–24). Detailed discussion of K-edge analysis is included in Supplementary Note 1, which shows that the sixth cation addition (Zn, Ga, Mg, and Al) induces edge shifts for Co and Fe, indicating oxidation state changes and T /O coordination. To further investigate the effect of sixth cation addition on cation redistribution, synchrotron XAS and X-ray magnetic circular dichroism (XMCD) were employed to examine electronic states and coordination (Supplementary Figs. 25–31). Figs. 2a, 2b show Co L-edge XAS and XMCD spectra of HESOs, together with the reference spectra of Co3+ O , Co2+ O and Co2+ T . All HESOs exhibit Co2+ and Co3+ features, but with different fine peak features. For example, Zn-HESO and Ga-HESO show distinct XAS and XMCD signatures. The XAS spectra show peak shift and broadening compared to the other HESOs, and XMCD provides element-specific magnetic contrast and differentiates oxidation states and site occupancies. Notably, the XMCD spectra for Zn- and Ga-HESO show clear signal combinations due to the co-existence of different valence occupancies. Spectral quantification using XAS spectra (Fig. 2c, Supplementary Fig. 26) shows that Al-HESO and Mg-HESO have more Co2+ in T sites, but Ga-HESO and Zn-HESO have more Co2+ and Co3+ in O sites. This is consistent with the cation preference (Fig. 1b) as Zn2+ and Ga3+ have a stronger T preference than Co ions. Figs. 2d-f show Fe L-edge XAS and XMCD with the reference spectra of Fe2+ O , Fe3+ O , and Fe3+ T , and fitted results for HESO and M-HESOs. HESO has the most Fe3+ in T sites and Fe2+ in O sites, while M-HESOs show an increased amount of Fe3+ in O (Fig. 2f). Similarly, XAS and XMCD analysis of Mn, Ni, Cr, and O (Supplementary Note 2) reveal that Mn, Cr, and Ni maintain their oxidation states and site occupancies across different HESOs. The modified cation distribution leads to a change in configurational entropy (ΔS ) (Fig. 2g-i). The pristine HESO has ΔS of 1.07R and 1.47R for T and O sites, while those for Zn-HESO are increased to 1.37R and 1.59R due to a more balanced cation distribution. The increased ΔS values for Zn-HESO are expected to increase phase stability (Supplementary Fig. 32).

Theoretical Investigation of the Effect of Zn Addition on Co Cation Distribution in HESO
To verify the experimental observation that Zn addition displaces Co from T to O sites (Fig. 2h), DFT calculations were performed. We employed the simple active site local impurity model from our previous work on HEOs.40 This model is based on a (100) facet surface slab of bulk Co O spinel, with a Co O active site fixed on the surface whose neighboring metals are interchanged amongst five elements (Fig. 3a). The local impurity model maintains the Co active site in Zn-HESO but substitutes Zn for one neighboring atom, either in O (Fig. 3b) or T (Fig. 3c). For the 120 pristine HESO Co-active-site permutations, Zn can either occupy O or T sites for each permutation, leading to 240 local impurity Zn-HESO configurations. Fig. 3d (Supplementary Table 1) shows total-energy histograms for Zn replacing Co, Ni, Mn, Fe, or Cr in T (top row) and O (bottom row) sites. Energies were corrected by adding 1/3 the energy of the pure M O spinel for each metal atom M replaced by Zn to allow comparison across different stoichiometries. Across all five substitutions, the mean energy of Zn in T sites is ~1.155-1.360 eV lower than in the corresponding Zn in O cases. Additionally, the structures where Zn replaces T Co sites show the lowest mean energy, 0.14 eV lower than the second lowest energy structures (Mn T sites). This indicates that Zn likely preferentially occupies T over O sites, consistent with site preference energy from crystal field theory (Fig. 1b),42 and that Zn may specifically displace Co from T , consistent with XAS/XMCD (Fig. 2h).

While the local impurity Zn-HESO model enables direct comparison with our previous HESO study, it simplifies the real structure by using Co O (100) as the support and assuming a normal spinel. To validate this model, we removed these simplifications (Supplementary Note 5) and developed a full high-entropy bulk Zn-HESO model. Fig. 3e shows a representative six-metal rhombohedral primitive cell with Zn and Fe in T and Co, Mn, Cr, and Ni in O . The energy histograms (Fig. 3f) show Zn T has a lower average energy than Zn O , in agreement with the simple-model result (Fig. 4d). We evaluated converged bulk configurations spanning normal, mixed normal/inverse, and inverse spinels with both CFT and DFT, and they show similar trends. The five most stable structures in descending order are (Co2Zn2) (Cr3Mn4Fe3Ni2) , (Fe3Zn2) (Cr3Mn3Co3Ni2) , (Fe3Zn2) (Cr3Mn4Co2Ni2) , (Ni2Zn2) (Cr3Mn4Fe3Co3) , and (Fe2Zn2) (Cr3Mn4Co3Ni2) (Supplementary Table 4). In this notation, superscripts represent oxidation state; the first two elements in T positions and the last four in O positions. In all five structures, Zn occupies the T site and Co2+ prefers the O site, matching XAS and XMCD element distributions (Fig. 2c). Mn4+ prefers the O site, consistent with XAS analysis (Supplementary Fig. 27). Notably, fully high-entropy bulk structures have similar bond lengths/angles as pure spinels (Co O , Fe O , Ni O , Mn O , Cr O ), indicating changes in OER behavior of Zn-HESO compared to pure spinels arise from electronic effects.

Theoretical DFT Investigation of the OER Activity for Zn-HESO
Since Co3+ is an established active site for OER,43 we further study how Zn-HESO-induced modulation in Co distribution affects its OER activity through DFT calculations and experiments. For DFT calculations, we used a fully high-entropy bulk model of the most stable Zn-HESOs (Fig. 3e) to form an O -terminated (100) surface (Fig. 4a), analogous to the simplified local impurity Zn-HESO model (Fig. 3b-c). We calculated O*, OH*, and selected OOH* adsorption energies on the most stable surfaces of both fully high-entropy Zn-HESO (Supplementary Table 4) and local impurity Zn-HESO model (Supplementary Table 1). Calculations follow the single-site OER pathway (Fig. 4b): a clean active site sequentially binds OH*, O*, and OOH*, then releases O to regenerate the site, recovering a clean catalyst surface. Although a direct O-O coupling route can be favored over the single-site mechanism, the overpotential calculated serves as a good lower bound on activity.

The volcano plot in Fig. 4c summarizes OER overpotentials for Co and non-Co active sites in HESO and Zn-HESO. It includes 24 local impurity Zn-HESO cases with Zn substituting T Co (Fig. 3c), paired with 24 pristine HESO surfaces from previous work40 to see the Zn substitution effect. Fig. 4c also includes 12 stable fully high-entropy Zn-HESO surfaces with Co and other cations as active sites, and the use of a fully high-entropy model to check the accuracy of the simpler impurity model. The calculated OER activity from the Co site local impurity model shows that Zn-HESOs (pink squares) are comparable to pristine HESOs (blue circles) (Supplementary Fig. 33-34), indicating that Zn does not have a large impact on the activity of individual Co sites. The scaling relationship between O*/OH*/OOH* (Supplementary Fig. 35) remains largely unchanged with a few Co outliers. We used the fully high-entropy models to evaluate Zn-HESOs with Co at O . The calculated overpotentials of Co3+ sites range from 350-540 mV, compared to 410-940 mV for Co sites in the local impurity model, indicating a smaller lower bound than the fully high-entropy model. The Co3+ O in the complex Zn-HESO model has an average overpotential of 453 mV, about 788 mV lower than that for Co2+. We also considered the possibility of other cations as potential active sites, with the most stable Zn-HESO with Co T , where it is not available as an active site. Among the calculated activities of four O sites (Ni, Fe, Mn, Cr), Cr has the lowest overpotential of 670 mV, but it is still larger than the best Co3+. The overpotentials of Fe, Mn, and Ni sites are 760 mV, 940 mV, and 1120 mV, respectively. Altogether, these results indicate that Co3+ O is the most active site for OER in Zn-HESO. Since Zn-HESOs have a slightly higher amount of Co3+ O than HESOs (Fig. 2c), we expect that Zn-HESO will be more active for OER (Figs. 5a-5c). While more Co3+ O sites will increase the activity, aligning with our expectations of improvement of Zn-HESO compared to pristine HESO, it is also important to note that the likely optimal Co occupation is less than 100%, as having the high entropy structure does lead to lower overpotentials than a pure Co spinel.

As electrical conductivity also impacts electrocatalytic performance, we examined the projected density of states (PDOS) of the five most stable bulk Zn-HESOs (Supplementary Fig. 36) to evaluate the impact of Zn substitution on conductivity. For four structures with O Co ((Fe3Zn2) (Cr3Mn3Co3Ni2) , (Fe3Zn2) (Cr3Mn4Co2Ni2) , (Ni2Zn2) (Cr3Mn4Fe3Co3) , and (Fe2Zn2) (Cr3Mn4Co3Ni2) ), the presence of Co states near the Fermi energy indicates that Co has available electrons for OER active site and is likely an active site. Additionally, PDOS plots for Co2+ O in (Fe3Zn2) (Cr3Mn4Co2Ni2) , have a much smaller band gap than those with Co3+ O sites in (Fe3Zn2) (Cr3Mn3Co3Ni2) , (Ni2Zn2) (Cr3Mn4Fe3Co3) , and (Fe2Zn2) (Cr3Mn4Co3Ni2) . This suggests that HESOs with more Co2+ O rather than Co 3+ are more conductive, because Co2+ provides an extra electron in comparison to Co3+ in n-type semiconductors like Zn-HESOs. As our experiments have shown an increase in Co2+ O from 20% in pristine HESOs to 60% in Zn-HESOs (Fig. 2c), we expect that Zn-HESO will show higher electrical conductivity than HESO (Fig. 5d).

Electrochemical performance of high-entropy spinel oxides for OER
To validate the DFT predictions that Zn-HESOs show more active and conductive, we experimentally measured OER properties of pristine HESO and M-HESOs (M = Zn, Ga, Mg, Al) in 1 M KOH electrolyte (Fig. 5). Fig. 5a plots iR-corrected polarization curves for pristine HESO, M-HESOs, and two references (CoFe O and Co O ). Among the substituted catalysts, Ga-HESO shows slightly lower onset overpotential at low current densities, consistent with its relatively strong tetrahedral site preference energy, which promotes effective redistribution of Co and Fe into octahedral coordination. However, this advantage is primarily observed in the low-current region. In contrast, Zn-HESO exhibits the lowest average overpotentials at both 10 mA cm-2 (η , 295 mV) and 100 mA cm-2 (η , 314 mV) (Supplementary Fig. 37), indicating great performance across a broader operational current range. The kinetic advantage of Zn-HESO is further evidenced by its lowest Tafel slope (25 mV dec-1) compared to Ga-HESO (37 mV dec-1), pristine HESO (33 mV dec-1), Mg-HESO (40 mV dec-1), and Al-HESO (45 mV dec-1) (Fig. 5b). This trend is directly reflected in the systematic increase in Tafel slopes from Zn- to Al-substituted systems, indicating progressively slower OER kinetics. In parallel, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (Fig. 5c) shows that Zn-HESO possesses the smallest charge transfer resistance (R ) from the Nyquist semicircle in electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS, Fig. 5c), and the double-layer capacitance (C ) of 1.8 mF cm-2 (Supplementary Figs. 38-39), indicating a larger electrochemical surface area (ECSA) of ~6 cm2. Importantly, after normalization by ECSA, Zn-HESO still exhibits a comparable or higher current density in the OER-relevant potential region. This observation suggests that factors beyond the electrochemically accessible surface area may influence the measured current density, such as differences in intrinsic catalytic reactivity, charge-transfer kinetics, surface electronic structure, or local reaction environments under OER conditions, as well as variations in ion accessibility, and the effective utilization of the catalyst surface. Benchmarking η , η , and Tafel slopes against literature-reported high-entropy OER catalysts ( Supplementary Fig. 40) positions Zn-HESO with one of the lowest Tafel slopes among state-of-the-art materials in both spinel and perovskite HEO classes.

The OER-related properties rank in the order of Zn-HESO > Ga-HESO > HESO > Mg-HESO > Al-HESO, the same order as the T preference energy of those added cations (Fig. 1b). This trend makes sense as DFT suggests that Co3+ O sites are the primary active sites for OER; the ranking reflects the ability of those added cations in pushing Co into O sites. The difference is more obvious at higher current density, which comes from the conductivity difference. The bulk electrical conductivity of Zn-HESO measured using the two-terminal method (Fig. 5d) is 0.17 mS cm-1, higher than pristine HESO (0.12 mS cm-1). This result is consistent with DFT DOS calculation (Supplementary Fig. 36) as structures with higher amounts of Co2+ O had a higher conductivity than structures with less Co2+ O . As the DFT calculation suggests that Co3+ O (Fig. 4c) is the dominant active site, both η and η of pristine and M-HESOs indeed show clear correlations with Co3+ and Co2+ O occupancy (Fig. 5e and Supplementary Fig. 41), but no clear correlation with Fe2+ and Fe3+ in either O or T (Supplementary Fig. 42). These results demonstrate that targeted enrichment of catalytically active Co in O correlates with enhanced OER performance. Finally, long-term durability was assessed via chronopotentiometry dynamically at 10 and 100 mA cm-2 (Fig. 5f). Zn-HESO maintains a stable overpotential over 80 hours of continuous operation (Fig. 5g). A slight and abrupt potential change observed at approximately 70 h arises from a routine maintenance step during the measurement, during which accumulated oxygen bubbles were removed from the electrode surface and the electrolyte was refreshed to ensure stable mass transport, rather than from catalyst degradation. Extended measurements further confirm similar stability up to ~120 hours at 10 mA cm-2 (Supplementary Fig. 43). In contrast, pristine HESO exhibits gradual performance degradation, particularly at high current density. The enhanced OER stability in Zn-HESO may be associated with a more homogeneous cation distribution across the spinel lattice (Fig. 2h), which could mitigate local compositional fluctuations and thereby improve structural robustness under OER conditions.

Operando XAS for Redox Dynamics of Co and Ni in Zn-HESO under OER Conditions
To probe redox dynamics of active sites for Zn-HESO during OER, we performed operando XAS in total fluorescence yield under electrochemical bias. Fig. 6a shows a custom-built three-electrode flow cell (Fig. 6a), where Zn-HESO-coated Ti/Pt/Si N electrodes were irradiated with X-rays, and Co and Ni L -edge signals were collected with circulating electrolyte. CV of Zn-HESO in 0.05 M KOH (Fig. 6b) revealed characteristic redox peaks between 0.8–1.2 V , indicating electrochemical activation of the catalyst surface, with OER onset beyond 1.45 V . Operando Co L -edge spectra (Fig. 6c) were recorded during a potential sweep starting from open circuit voltage (OCV, ~0.8 V ), increasing anodically to 1.45 V , and reversing back to reduction potentials. At an initial 0.8 V , Co L -edge peaks at ~779.2 eV, corresponding to mixed Co2+/Co3+ species. As potential increases, Co peak shifts progressively to higher photon energies, reaching a maximum at 1.45 V , indicating oxidation of Co2+ to Co3+ and formation of CoOOH-like species under OER-relevant conditions.44,45 During the cathodic sweep, Co L -edge shifts back toward lower energies, reflecting partial reduction to Co2+. Notably, Co spectra at 0.8 V after the cathodic sweep did not fully recover to the initial state, suggesting partial irreversibility or restructuring of the Co environment. This partial irreversibility indicates that while Co undergoes dynamic redox transitions, some oxidized Co species remain stabilized after high-potential cycling, potentially contributing to catalyst activation. Similarly, Ni L -edge spectra (Fig. 6d) exhibit oxidation from Ni2+ to Ni3+ under anodic polarization, with the most significant shifts near 1.2–1.45 V , and partial reduction during the cathodic sweep with some hysteresis.45,46 Such observed redox hysteresis likely reflects structural or electronic reconfigurations associated with transition metal (oxy)hydroxide formation under OER. While Co has been widely identified as the primary redox-active species, our operando XAS measurements also reveal a subtle shift in Ni edge position, indicating its partial involvement in electronic reorganization. This suggests that Ni may play a secondary or synergistic role during catalysis. The complex redox behavior in high-entropy systems reveals limitations of attributing catalytic activity to a single element, emphasizing the need for comprehensive, site-resolved, multi-element analysis.

Consistent with these operando L-edge observations, previously reported operando K-edge XANES studies on closely related high-entropy spinel oxides show that the Co K-edge shifts toward higher photon energies under anodic polarization, while the Ni K-edge exhibits a weaker but discernible shift toward higher oxidation states. These K-edge results further support the interpretation that Co undergoes pronounced redox evolution under OER conditions, with Ni contributing subtly to the overall electronic reorganization.47

Integrating experiments and theory, we showed that coordinate-site engineering enables controlled tuning of cation distributions in HESOs. Zn, with the strongest T preference, is associated with increased Co occupancy in O . Quantitative site occupancies aligned well with DFT and suggest Co3+ at O as the dominant active site for OER. The high-current performance of Zn-HESO is consistent with higher electronic conductivity, which correlates with a greater fraction of electron-donating Co2+ at O . Fully high-entropy models indicate mixed normal/inverse spinel configurations whose site populations are adjustable via Zn, offering a potential explanation for experimentally observed site distributions. Lastly, operando spectroscopy reveals partially reversible Co/Ni oxidation under OER, supporting sustained activity. Our investigations challenge assumptions of sublattice homogeneity and establish targeted elements as an effective lever for site and valence distributions and enhance catalytic performance.

## Methods

Synthesis of spinel oxides and HEOs.
All chemicals were used as purchased without further purification. The metal precursors—chromium (III) nitrate nonahydrate, manganese (II) nitrate tetrahydrate, iron (II) nitrate hexahydrate, nickel (II) nitrate hexahydrate, and cobalt (II) nitrate (all from Sigma-Aldrich)—were used to prepare the spinel oxides. Absolute ethanol (99.5+%, Acros Organics) was used as the solvent. Potassium hydroxide (reagent grade, 90%, Sigma-Aldrich) was used as the electrolyte for electrochemical measurements. All spinel oxides studied in this work were synthesized using a previously reported, rapid sol–gel flame method. Equimolar concentrations (0.1 M) of each metal precursor were dissolved in ethanol and sonicated for 30 minutes to ensure complete mixing. The precursor solution was then spin-coated onto clean fluorine-doped tin oxide (FTO) glass substrates (7–8 Ω/sq, MSE Supplies) at 3000 rpm for 30 seconds, followed by annealing on a hot plate at 120 °C. This spin-coating and annealing process was repeated twice to achieve uniform film coverage. The precursor-coated FTO/glass substrates were annealed in the post-flame region of a co-flow premixed flat-flame burner (McKenna Burner). The burner operated using premixed methane (CH ) as fuel and air as oxidizer, with a fuel-to-oxygen equivalence ratio of 1.0. The substrates were positioned 3 cm above the burner surface and exposed to the flame for 45 seconds, during which the local gas temperature reached approximately 1000 °C, as measured by a K-type thermocouple (1/16 in. bead size, Omega Engineering, Inc.). After flame annealing, the samples were removed from the flame and allowed to cool naturally to room temperature (25 °C). This rapid high-temperature heating and cooling cycle facilitates homogeneous multi-elemental mixing and stabilizes the high-entropy spinel phases.

Materials characterizations.
The crystal structure of the synthesized samples was characterized using X-ray diffraction (XRD, PANalytical Empyrean) equipped with a Cu Kα radiation source (λ = 1.54 Å). Surface chemical composition and elemental quantification were analyzed by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, PHI VersaProbe 3) using a monochromated Al Kα source (1486 eV). High-resolution imaging, dark-field imaging, and elemental mapping via energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) were performed using a scanning transmission electron microscope (STEM, Thermo Fisher Spectra).

Electronic structure analysis through synchrotron X-ray absorption spectroscopy at the K-edge
To investigate the bulk valence states of Fe and Co, X- ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) measurements were performed in transmission mode at beamline 4-1 of the Stanford Synchrotron Radiation Lightsource (SSRL). Samples were sealed under argon in pouch cells to prevent air exposure. A Si (220) monochromator (ϕ = 90°) was used and detuned to 50–60% of the peak intensity to suppress higher-order harmonics. Photon energy calibration was carried out using Fe reference foils by setting the zero-crossing point of the second derivative of the absorption spectrum to 7112 eV. Three ion chambers arranged in series were used to record the incident (I ), transmitted (I ), and reference (I ) intensities. Spectrum alignment and normalization were performed using the Athena software package, while XAS data fitting and simulations were carried out using Artemis.

Electronic structure analysis through synchrotron X-ray absorption spectroscopy and X-ray magnetic circular dichroism at the L-edge
To obtain element-specific magnetic information, we performed X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) and X-ray magnetic circular dichroism (XMCD) measurements at the L -edges of all transition metals using the total electron yield (TEY) detection mode. All experiments were carried out at beamline 13-3 of the Stanford Synchrotron Radiation Lightsource (SSRL). Measurements were conducted in normal incidence geometry with an incident angle set at 90°. The samples were cooled in a closed-cycle helium liquefied system and maintained at a base temperature of 13.5 K,48 which is well below Curie temperature (T ). We obtained the absorption spectra by reversing the X-ray polarity (right and left circular – RCP and LCP) of the incident photon beam, while a constant external magnetic field of approximately 0.4 T along the surface normal direction was applied using a neodymium permanent magnet. The XMCD signal was obtained by taking the difference between RCP and LCP spectra. To quantitatively determine the valence- and site-specific distributions of Co and Fe in the spinel lattice, Co and Fe L-edge XAS spectra were analyzed using a linear-combination fitting approach based on ligand-field multiplet–simulated reference spectra. Although experimentally measured Co and Fe L-edge spectra of representative spinel oxides were acquired and are shown for qualitative comparison (Supplementary Fig. 25, 30, 31), such reference materials inherently contain mixed tetrahedral and octahedral site occupancies as well as mixed oxidation states and therefore cannot serve as isolated standards for site-resolved quantification. Accordingly, site- and valence-specific reference spectra corresponding to Co3+(O ), Co2+(O ), Co2+(T ), Fe2+(O ), Fe3+(O ), or Fe3+(T ) were taken from well-established ligand-field multiplet–simulated datasets reported in the literature.49–51 For the quantification, all experimental L-edge spectra were energy-aligned, background-subtracted, and normalized to the edge jump prior to analysis. The experimental spectrum for each sample, W(E), was then modeled as a linear combination of the normalized reference spectra according to
𝑊(𝐸) = ∑ 𝑎 𝑋 (𝐸) (1)
, where X(E) denotes the reference spectra and a are non-negative fitting coefficients constrained to sum to unity. The fitting was performed by least-squares minimization using the Trust-Region Reflective algorithm implemented in MATLAB. The uncertainties in the extracted site fractions were determined as the 95% confidence intervals derived from the regression covariance matrix. XMCD spectra were additionally used as a complementary constraint to distinguish tetrahedral and octahedral contributions, owing to their distinct magnetic signatures.

Operando XAS on Co and Ni Redox Dynamics in Zn-HESO
Operando X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) experiments were carried out at beamline 8.0.1 of the Advanced Light Source (ALS) located at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL). During measurements, the storage ring operated at an energy of 1.9 GeV with a beam current close to 500 mA. Spectra were collected in total fluorescence yield (TFY) mode. The energy windows used for data acquisition were 774–790 eV for the Co L₃-edge and 845–860 eV for the Ni L -edge. To ensure accurate normalization, the incident X-ray intensity (I ) was continuously monitored using the drain current of an upstream gold-coated mesh while TFY signals were recorded simultaneously. A custom electrochemical flow cell was employed for operando measurements. The cell incorporated a 100 nm-thick silicon nitride membrane that maintained separation between the liquid electrolyte and the high-vacuum chamber. To prepare the working electrode, a 5 nm titanium adhesion layer was first deposited onto the membrane, followed by a 10 nm platinum conductive layer. The active material, Zn-HESO, was subsequently loaded onto the platinum surface through a drop-casting process. For ink preparation, Zn-HESO powder was dispersed in ethanol (3 mg mL-1) and ultrasonicated until a uniform suspension was obtained. A 10 μL portion of the suspension was then deposited onto the electrode surface and dried at 60 °C. This coating procedure was repeated 25 times to achieve sufficient loading, after which the electrode underwent thermal treatment at 150 °C for 1 hour.

Electrochemical testing was performed using a three-electrode configuration consisting of an Ag/AgCl reference electrode and a platinum counter electrode. All measurements were conducted in 0.05 M KOH electrolyte with a BioLogic SP-200 potentiostat. Images of the operando XAS electrochemical flow-cell assembly are presented in Supplementary Fig. 46.

Electrochemical measurement
All electrochemical measurements—including linear sweep voltammetry (LSV), cyclic voltammetry (CV), chronopotentiometry (CP), and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS)—were performed using a potentiostat (Interface 1010, Gamry Instruments) in a standard three-electrode setup. The electrolyte used was 30 mL of 1 M KOH (pH ~14), and its pH was measured using a calibrated benchtop pH meter (Mettler Toledo F20-Kit). Calibration was conducted prior to measurements using standard buffer solutions of pH 4, 7, and 10. The 1 M KOH electrolyte was prepared by dissolving potassium hydroxide (reagent grade, 90%, Sigma-Aldrich) in deionized water. The solution was freshly prepared prior to each experiment and stored in a tightly sealed polypropylene bottle to minimize CO absorption. The synthesized spinel oxides served as working electrodes with a geometric area of 0.196 cm-2. A platinum wire and an Hg/HgO electrode were used as counter and reference electrodes, respectively. All measured potentials versus Hg/HgO were converted to the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) scale using the equation:
E = E + 0.059 × pH + 0.098 (2)
LSV curves were recorded at a scan rate of 10 mV s-1 and corrected for 85% of the solution resistance (iR compensation). Overpotentials (η) were calculated as:
η=E −1.23 V (3)
Tafel plots were constructed by plotting overpotential (η) versus the logarithm of the current density (log j). Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was carried out over a frequency range of 20 kHz to 0.05 kHz at 1.54 V . The EIS measurements consist of solution resistance (R ), charge-transfer resistance (R ), and double-layer capacitance (C ). The HESO and M-HESO electrodes exhibit R values in the range of 15–25 Ω, which were used for the iR compensation.

Long-term electrochemical stability was evaluated using chronopotentiometry at initial current densities of ~10 and 100 mA cm-2. The electrochemical surface area (ECSA) was estimated via CV measurements in non-Faradaic regions at varying scan rates and calculated using the equation; ECSA=C /Cs, where C is the specific capacitance of a smooth surface in alkaline media, taken as 60 μF cm-2.

Electrical conductivity measurements
The electrical conductivity of pressed powder pellets was measured using a two-electrode configuration on a potentiostat (Interface 1010, Gamry Instruments). Powder samples were first pressed into cylindrical pellets using a uniaxial press at a load corresponding to 10 MPa. Before each measurement, the baseline resistance of the measurement system was determined by assembling the fixture without a sample. The fixture consisted of samples embedded in a Teflon die. The thickness between the metal plates was measured with calibrated digital calipers (repeated 5 times to average), ensuring that the calipers were zeroed before each measurement.

For conductivity measurements, the pellet was placed between the metal electrode and the stopper in the Teflon holder, then compressed to 10 MPa. The load was maintained for approximately 1 min to allow stabilization, with additional pressure applied if the value decreased. The sample thickness was measured at the same points as in the baseline measurement, and the baseline thickness was subtracted to obtain the net sample thickness.

Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) was performed to determine the total system resistance, with sweep rate parameters adjusted according to the expected sample conductivity (e.g., 1000 mV s-1 for low-conductivity samples, 10 mV s-1 for high-conductivity samples).

The slope of the current–voltage curve was determined for both the baseline and the sample measurement. The sample contribution was calculated according to:
𝑠𝑎𝑚𝑝𝑙𝑒 𝑠𝑙𝑜𝑝𝑒 = (1/𝑠𝑎𝑚𝑝𝑙𝑒 𝑠𝑦𝑠𝑡𝑒𝑚 𝑠𝑙𝑜𝑝𝑒 − 1/𝑏𝑎𝑠𝑒𝑙𝑖𝑛𝑒 𝑠𝑦𝑠𝑡𝑒𝑚 𝑠𝑙𝑜𝑝𝑒) (4)
The electrical conductivity, 𝜎 (S cm⁻¹), was then obtained using:
σ = (𝑠𝑙𝑜𝑝𝑒 [A/V] × 𝑡ℎ𝑖𝑐𝑘𝑛𝑒𝑠𝑠 [𝑐𝑚]) / 𝑎𝑟𝑒𝑎 [𝑐𝑚]2 (5)

Computational Details. We follow a similar DFT calculation scheme and parameters as in our previous HEO spinel work, which we briefly summarize here.40 We performed spin-polarized density functional theory calculations with a plane-wave basis set using the Vienna ab initio simulation package (VASP)52,53 and project augmented wave (PAW) pseudopotential,54 and we conducted and analyzed all calculations using the atomic simulation environment (ASE).55 We described electronic exchange and correlation using the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof functional.56 We applied the DFT+U method and set the energy cutoff to 600 eV for all calculations. The complex six-element Zn-HESO bulk structures were optimized using 5x5x5 k-point mesh sampling, and considered their bulk structures optimal when the energies and forces dropped below 10-5 eV and 0.02 eV/Å, respectively. Fully high-entropy Zn-HESO OER calculations were performed on (100) surfaces with three frozen atomic layers and two free layers. Initial magnetic moments were applied to achieve targeted spin states on each element by setting the occupation matrix of 3d-electron localization, followed by optimizing the geometry.57

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

This manuscript presents a thorough study on tuning cation site occupancy in high-entropy spinel oxides via incorporation of a sixth element (Zn, Ga, Al, Mg). Using synchrotron XAS/XMCD and DFT calculations, the authors demonstrated Zn's preference for tetrahedral sites, which redistributed Co to octahedral sites, enhancing the electronic conductivity and OER performance. This work is well-supported by extensive characterization data and addresses an important topic in catalyst design.
However, the electrochemical analysis lacks rigor, with serious flaws in iR compensation, ECSA determination, and stability testing undermining the reliability of the performance claims. The justification for using high-entropy systems over simpler analogs also requires strengthening. While the core findings are valuable, these issues must be addressed to validate the conclusions.
1. The manuscript should provide a stronger justification for employing HESO in this coordination site study, explicitly addressing why this complex platform offers advantages over simpler, well-defined binary or ternary spinel systems. Additionally, the potential influence of the sixth cation on other key OER-active elements (Ni, Fe) should be thoroughly addressed.
2. The LSV curves in Figure 5a appear to be overcompensated, resulting in distorted data. The resistance value used for iR-correction must be determined by electrochemical testing, and the specific value should be clearly annotated in the figure. The inset in Figure 5g also shows clear signs of overcompensation.
3. The Tafel slopes in Figure 5b appear to be derived from an inappropriate fitting range, potentially including data from both the low-current-density and high-current-density non-linear regions. This practice can distort the slope value and misrepresent the catalytic kinetics.
4. The data presented do not sufficiently support the conclusion that Zn-HESO is the optimal catalyst. As shown in Figure 5a, Ga-HESO clearly demonstrates superior activity at lower current densities, an observation further compounded by the apparently overcompensated LSV curve of Zn-HESO. This performance trend is corroborated by the Tafel analysis in Figure 5b. The authors should either re-perform these electrochemical measurements to ensure data integrity or provide additional analyses to substantiate the claimed performance hierarchy.
5. For the operando sXAS analysis in Figure 6, a photograph of the actual electrochemical flow cell setup used for the measurements should be provided in the supplementary information.
6. The selection of scan rates (20, 50, 100, 200, and 300 mV/s) in Supplementary Fig. 29 appears to be nonstandard for capacitance determination, and the varying voltage windows across different materials undermine meaningful ECSA comparisons. The absence of 20 mV/s data for HESO requires explanation. These issues should be addressed to validate the ECSA analysis.
7. The abrupt change in the chronopotentiometry data at approximately 70 hours in Figure 5g requires explanation.

### Reviewer 2

This manuscript presents an extensive study on coordination-site engineering in high-entropy spinel oxides of Co-Fe-Cr-Mn-Ni by introducing an element of Zn, Ga, Mg, or Al. The authors carried out XAS/XMCD, DFT calculations, and electrochemical measurements to show that Zn incorporation redistributes Co from tetrahedral to octahedral sites enhancing OER activity. The concept of entropy-driven site modulation is very interesting and innovative. I recommend that this manuscript can be considered for publication in Nature Communications after appropriate revisions. Several key points need to be reconsidered or revised, as detailed below.
1) While the authors mention that Co L3-edge and Fe L3-edge XAS spectra were obtained for reference samples of Co3+ (Oh), Co2+(Oh), Co2+(Td), Fe2+(Oh), Fe3+(Oh), and Fe3+(Td)” in Fig. 2, the manuscript does not specify which compounds were used to obtain these reference spectra. The corresponding reference materials should be clearly described in the main manuscript.
2) All relevant spinel-type reference compounds should be measured by both hard XAS and soft XAS for all elements. For example, in the case of Fe K-edge and Fe L-edge XAS, MnFe2O4, CoFe2O4, NiFe2O4, and ZnFe2O4 would be useful to discuss Fe valence and tetrahedral/octahedral coordination. Similarly, for Ni K-edge and L-edge XAS, NiFe2O4 is also informative. I recommend that the authors discuss the valence states and Td/Oh coordination environments in more detail using such references.
3) In the Co K-edge and Fe K-edge XAFS spectra in Figures S9 and S10, the differences among Zn-, Ga-, Mg-, Al-substituted and pristine HESO samples are not clearly visible.
It is difficult to identify the valence shift of Co and Fe induced by the sixth-element doping.
4) In the EXAFS spectra in Figures S9-S13, spectra of appropriate reference compounds should be included for comparison of local coordination structures.
5) Did the authors simulate the second-nearest coordination shell around 3A in Figure S14? This region appears to change depending on the type of sixth-element doping in Figures S9-S13.
6) The authors should perform detailed curve-fitting simulations for all samples (Zn-, Ga-, Mg-, Al-doped and pristine HESO) to quantitatively evaluate the structural parameters.
7) In this study, structural information of Zn and Ga is crucial. Please measure the Zn and Ga K-edge EXAFS spectra to confirm the local coordination of each element. The central hypothesis relies on Zn occupying Td sites, but the manuscript currently does not provide direct experimental verification.
8) While the authors claim a clear redistribution of Co and Fe between tetrahedral and octahedral sites upon Zn substitution, the quantitative reliability of the XAS/XMCD fitting is not fully demonstrated. The deconvolution and fitting procedures should be described in sufficient detail. This is quite important.
9) In Figure 6, the operando XAS spectra are not very clear due to the broad peaks. In the Co L3-edge spectra, a new feature appears near 782 eV at 0.8 V in the final measurement.
10) The authors should compare the operando Co K-edge and Ni K-edge XAFS spectra with the corresponding Co L-edge and Ni L-edge spectra in terms of valence shifts and local structural changes. Reference spectra of Co(OH)2, CoOOH, Ni(OH)2, and NiOOH would be useful for this discussion.
11) The authors should clarify how the L-edge XAS spectra allow distinguishing between octahedral and tetrahedral sites, since these spectral features are often similar and difficult to separate.

### Reviewer 3

In this study, Baet et al. investigate the effect of introducing a sixth cation into a Co-Fe-Cr-Mn-Ni HESO to modulate cation site occupancy. Among five candidate cations examined, Zn is identified as the most effective in altering the distribution of Co2+ and Co3+ ions between Td and Oh sites. The authors employ a combination of advanced characterization techniques and theoretical calculations to build a fundamental understanding of coordination environment control in HEOs. While the study is intriguing and the narrative is generally well-constructed, the OER performance of the optimized Zn-HESO catalyst falls short of the benchmark expected for publication in this journal. Therefore, despite the scientific merit of the work, I cannot recommend its publication in its current form. My major concerns are detailed below.
Major Comments:
1. The authors should provide details regarding the identification of Td and Oh sites in these HEOs via STEM.
2. TEM images for Al-HESO are missing. Based on HR-TEM, the authors identified that the interplanar spacing at the (311) plane for Mg-HESO and Ga-HESO is larger than that of HESO. However, the XRD patterns show that the (311) diffraction peak for both Mg-HESO and Ga-HESO shifts to higher angles, indicating a decrease in their interplanar spacing. Please clarify this apparent discrepancy.
3.In this work, the authors synthesized four distinct cation-engineered materials: Mg-HESO, Ga-HESO, Al-HESO, and Zn-HESO, each with different site occupancies. However, the discussion section primarily focuses on comparisons between HESO and Zn-HESO, lacking a detailed comparative discussion highlighting the differences among these high-entropy oxides.
4.The iR-corrected OER polarization curves presented in this manuscript show that Zn-HESO requires an overpotential of 295 mV to achieve 10 mA cm⁻2. Furthermore, the demonstrated stability duration is relatively short. Compared to similar OER studies published in Nature Communications, these performance metrics do not appear competitive.
5.The combined experimental and theoretical results indicate that Co3+ at the Oh site in Zn-HESO is the primary active center. Given this, is there an optimal proportion for the Co3+ Oh content in Zn-HESO?
Minor Comments:
1. The abbreviation ‘HEOs’ is used without being defined upon its first appearance in the introduction part.
2.The elemental percentages/compositions for Mg-HESO, Ga-HESO, and Al-HESO should also be provided, as demonstrated in supplementary Fig. 8.

5) Did the authors simulate the second-nearest coordination shell around 3A in Figure S14?
This region appears to change depending on the type of sixth-element doping in Figures S9-
S13.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer for raising this point. In high-entropy spinel oxides,
quantitative fitting of the second-shell EXAFS is intrinsically unreliable and therefore not
pursued. Unlike the first coordination shell, which corresponds to well-defined metal-oxygen
bonds, the second cation shell represents a chemically and structurally disordered ensemble of
multiple metal-metal pairs with similar scattering properties but distributed interatomic
distances. The random occupation of tetrahedral and octahedral sites by multiple transition
metals introduces substantial static disorder, leading to large Debye-Waller factors that strongly
damp higher-R EXAFS oscillations. In addition, second-shell single-scattering contributions
significantly overlap with multiple-scattering paths inherent to the spinel framework, further
obscuring path-specific signatures in R space. Combined with the limited backscattering
contrast among neighboring 3d transition metals and strong parameter correlations in multi-
path fitting, these factors render the extracted coordination numbers and distances non-unique
and highly model-dependent. As a result, we think the second-shell EXAFS in this system is
not appropriate for quantitative fitting.

The expanded EXAFS analysis reveals that site redistribution in doped high-entropy spinel
oxides is highly element-specific and governed by an interplay of crystal-field stabilization,
redox flexibility, and dopant site preference. Co is the most sensitive to sixth-cation substitution:
in pristine HESO, Co predominantly occupies tetrahedral (Td) sites, while Zn and Ga
substitution progressively drive Co toward octahedral (Oh) coordination, with Zn-HESO

redistribution energetically unfavorable.

concentrations, the absorption edge jump becomes very small, leading to a poor signal-to-noise
ratio. As a result, high-k oscillations are strongly suppressed, the effective k-range is

the Td and Oh sublattices are antiparallel. As reported in earlier studies of high-entropy spinel
oxides (e.g., Acta Mater. 2022, Sarkar et al.), the sign of the XMCD peak provides a direct
indicator of whether a cation predominantly occupies the Td or Oh site. In our case, Co and Fe
showed XMCD sign reversal consistent with the expected antiparallel coupling of Td and Oh
cations, enabling a robust assignment of the site fractions. We have included the Methods and
Discussion sections to clarify this procedure.
In this study, Baek et al. investigate the effect of introducing a sixth cation into a Co-Fe-Cr-
Mn-Ni HESO to modulate cation site occupancy. Among five candidate cations examined, Zn
is identified as the most effective in altering the distribution of Co2+ and Co3+ ions between
Td and Oh sites. The authors employ a combination of advanced characterization techniques
and theoretical calculations to build a fundamental understanding of coordination environment
control in HEOs. While the study is intriguing and the narrative is generally well-constructed,
the OER performance of the optimized Zn-HESO catalyst falls short of the benchmark
expected for publication in this journal. Therefore, despite the scientific merit of the work, I
cannot recommend its publication in its current form. My major concerns are detailed below.
Response: We truly appreciate the reviewer for the thoughtful evaluation of our work and for
recognizing the fundamental interest of coordination-site modulation in high-entropy oxides.
We appreciate the reviewer’s concerns regarding the OER performance of Zn-HESO and the
need for stronger evidence to support our conclusions. We would like to clarify that the primary
aim of this study is to uncover the fundamental thermodynamic and electronic principles
governing cation redistribution in high-entropy spinel oxides. Our focus is on understanding
how entropy-driven coordination-site modulation occurs and how these structural and
electronic changes correlate with catalytic behavior. While we agree that further optimization
of morphology, surface engineering, and nanoscale engineering could significantly enhance the
absolute OER activity, such catalyst-design efforts lie beyond the scope of the present
mechanistic study. Instead, our goal here is to provide a foundational and theory-based
understanding of site occupancy, electronic structure evolution, and the resulting activity trends
within a chemically complex multi-cation lattice. We hope this clarification helps contextualize
the performance levels observed and the scientific intent of the manuscript.
Major Comments:
1. The authors should provide details regarding the identification of Td and Oh sites in these
HEOs via STEM.
Response: We thank the reviewer for pointing this out. The Td and Oh labels in Fig. 1d are not
derived from atomic-resolution chemical identification, but from the projected geometry of the
spinel lattice along the [110] zone axis, which is well established in the literature for spinel
oxides. In a normal or inverse spinel viewed along [110], the oxygen sublattice forms a
34
characteristic zig-zag arrangement, and the tetrahedral and octahedral cation sites project into
distinct crystallographic positions in the image. Accordingly, the Td and Oh sites marked in
Fig. 1d correspond to theoretical lattice positions expected for the spinel structure when viewed
along [110], as confirmed by: (1) the crystallographic model of the spinel unit cell, (2) slice
image simulations of spinel viewed along [110] in Fig. 1c, and (3) prior reports demonstrating
the recognizable Td/Oh projected positions in spinels (e.g., Nanoscale Res. Lett. 2013, 8, 374).
Importantly, we clarify that these labels are only structural guides, indicating the expected
crystallographic positions of T and O sites. Quantitative determination of site populations
d h
was instead obtained from L-edge multiplet fitting, XMCD, and K-edge XANES/EXAFS,
as detailed in the main text.
2. TEM images for Al-HESO are missing. Based on HR-TEM, the authors identified that the
interplanar spacing at the (311) plane for Mg-HESO and Ga-HESO is larger than that of HESO.
However, the XRD patterns show that the (311) diffraction peak for both Mg-HESO and Ga-
HESO shifts to higher angles, indicating a decrease in their interplanar spacing. Please clarify
this apparent discrepancy.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this important comment. First, we have remeasured the
XRD patterns for all samples to clarify this point. The apparent inconsistency arises because
XRD provides ensemble-averaged lattice parameters over the entire sample, and the
remeasured XRD (311) peak shifts are actually very small (i.e., subtle changes in the bulk-
averaged lattice parameter), whereas HR-TEM lattice-fringe measurements reflect local d-
spacings from selected nanoscale regions that can be affected by local strain, compositional
fluctuation, and measurement uncertainty. According to Bragg’s law, a shift of the (311) peak
toward a higher 2θ indeed corresponds to a decrease in the average d(311). In our updated
XRD patterns, the (311) reflections of M-HESOs show slight shifts to higher angles compared
to pristine HESO, indicating a minor bulk-averaged contraction of the spinel lattice, while the
overall phase and peak set remain unchanged, confirming that the spinel framework is
preserved.
In HR-TEM, we measured local (311) lattice fringes and obtained d(311) = 0.254 nm (Ga-
HESO), 0.257 nm (Mg-HESO), 0.263 nm (Al-HESO), and 0.246 nm (Zn-HESO), all of which
fall within the characteristic range of the spinel (311) plane. Importantly, these values represent
local spacings in specific crystallites/regions rather than bulk averages. In compositionally
complex spinels, nanoscale strain accommodation and local lattice relaxation can produce
locally expanded fringes even when the bulk-averaged lattice parameter from XRD shows a
slight contraction. In addition, the small XRD peak shifts correspond to sub-percent changes
in d(311), which can be comparable to the uncertainty in extracting lattice fringes from HR-
TEM (e.g., local thickness/tilt/FFT selection), further amplifying the apparent difference when
comparing a single local value to an ensemble-averaged XRD position.
Therefore, the HR-TEM and XRD results are not contradictory but complementary: XRD
captures the ensemble-averaged crystallographic response, whereas HR-TEM highlights local
structural heterogeneity. We have revised the manuscript to explicitly clarify that HR-TEM-
derived d-spacings should not be interpreted as bulk lattice parameters. In addition, we now
include the missing HR-TEM images for Al-HESO, and the extracted d(311) is reported
alongside the other compositions.

Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s comment regarding the OER benchmarking. While
the overpotential of ~295 mV at 10 mA cm-2 is not among the very best values reported in
Nature Communications, the primary goal of this study is to establish a clear structure–property
correlation between entropy-driven cation redistribution and OER behavior in high-entropy
spinel oxide structures. Electrochemical performance is therefore used as a diagnostic probe to
validate the redistribution mechanism. We emphasize that the present materials were evaluated
40
without any morphology engineering, surface-area enhancement, or nano-structuring. These
well-known strategies typically yield substantial improvements in OER performance, and we
expect that applying them to Zn-HESO and Ga-HESO would further reduce overpotential.

another long-term stability data (Supplementary Fig. 42) shows continuous operation for
~120 hours at 10 mA cm-2 for both pristine HESO and Zn-HESO, with no observable
degradation trend.
